method: OPEN AND QUOTED from Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia' (2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328)). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10108006). Source text: the article abstract (tags stripped) followed by the body text from pmc_text.py, both from the Europe PMC JATS XML.

claims.claim: **TIO is a rare paraneoplastic syndrome:** mesenchymal tumours secrete FGF23, causing progressive bone pain, muscle weakness and fragility fractures.
claims.source_text: Tumor‐induced osteomalacia (TIO) is a rare paraneoplastic syndrome caused by mesenchymal tumors that secrete fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Patients present with progressive bone pain, muscle weakness, and fragility fractures.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **It is usually missed at first:** the initial misdiagnosis rate is 95.1%, and a delay of 2.5–3.5 years to tumour treatment has been reported (over 2 years in 80% of cases).
claims.source_text: TIO has an initial misdiagnosis rate of 95.1% … A delay of 2.5-3.5 years has recently been reported between initial presentation and tumor‐related treatment, with a delay of >2 years in 80% of cases
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Measure serum phosphate in anyone with chronic muscle pain or weakness, fragility fractures or bone pain.** It is not in standard chemistry panels, so it must be requested.
claims.source_text: Serum phosphate should be measured in patients presenting with chronic muscle pain or weakness, fragility fractures, or bone pain. … However, serum phosphate measurement is not typically included in standard chemistry panels [], so the clinician must think to order this test specifically.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine for myopathy and palpate the whole body for masses,** which are often very small.
claims.source_text: Physical examination should establish features of myopathy and identify masses that could be causative tumors. … The entire body should be palpated for masses [], which are often very small.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Take serum phosphate fasting in the morning and use an age-specific range.** In adults hypophosphataemia is below 0.8 mmol/L (2.5 mg/dL); chronic hypophosphataemia needs two low values at least 2 weeks apart.
claims.source_text: Serum phosphate should be measured on a morning, fasting blood specimen []. Serum phosphate concentration is normally higher in young children and decreases with age []; therefore, it is important to make sure that an age‐specific normal range is used. In adults, hypophosphatemia is defined as levels below 0.8 mmol/L (2.5 mg/dL) []. To establish chronic hypophosphatemia, there must be two values below the normal range on at least two occasions ≥2 weeks apart.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Full panel:** blood count, fasting phosphate, creatinine, calcium, albumin and total ALP, plus PTH, 25(OH)D, 1,25(OH)2D and FGF23.
claims.source_text: Comprehensive laboratory evaluation should include complete blood count, fasting serum phosphate, serum creatinine, calcium, albumin, and total alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Additional variables, including PTH, 25(OH)D, 1,25(OH)2D, and FGF23, should also be measured
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Confirm renal phosphate wasting:** collect fasting serum and second-morning-void urine phosphate and creatinine together, and calculate TRP and TmP/GFR. A low TmP/GFR or %TRP raises suspicion of TIO.
claims.source_text: Simultaneous fasting serum phosphate and creatinine, and urine phosphate and creatinine (second morning void) should be collected to assess renal phosphate reabsorption … Hypophosphatemia with low TmP/GFR and/or %TRP should raise suspicion for TIO
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Vitamin D deficiency does not rule TIO out.** Hypophosphataemia that persists after vitamin D is corrected should prompt consideration of TIO.
claims.source_text: However, vitamin D deficiency/insufficiency is frequent in the general population, and a low 25(OH)D level does not rule out the possibility of concurrent TIO. In fact, persistent hypophosphatemia after correction of vitamin D deficiency should prompt consideration that the patient may have TIO.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **1,25(OH)2D is typically low or inappropriately normal.** Interpret FGF23 with caution (assays are not standardised); a low or low-normal FGF23 points away from TIO.
claims.source_text: 1,25(OH)2D is typically low or inappropriately normal in patients with TIO [, ] because FGF23 reduced its synthesis and increases its catabolism. … Additionally, FGF23 assays are not standardized and can provide variable results for intact FGF23 measurement … If intact or C‐terminal FGF23 is low or low normal, the clinician should consider diagnoses other than TIO.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer once renal phosphate wasting and TIO are suspected** to a metabolic bone specialist or endocrinologist at a centre experienced in TIO.
claims.source_text: Once the presence of chronic hypophosphatemia due to excess renal phosphate excretion and TIO is suspected, patients should be referred to an appropriate specialist (such as a metabolic bone specialist or endocrinologist) at secondary or tertiary centers with experience in treating TIO for diagnosis confirmation
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Genetic testing:** ideally in all children and young adults suspected of TIO, and strongly considered in adults with renal phosphate wasting, especially when no tumour is found.
claims.source_text: Ideally, all children and young adults suspected of having TIO should undergo genetic testing to exclude genetic causes of hypophosphatemia. Because the onset of heritable causes can sometimes be subtle, not becoming apparent until adulthood, genetic testing should be strongly considered in adults with chronic hypophosphatemia due to renal phosphate wasting for whom the diagnosis of TIO is being considered, especially when the tumor cannot be identified.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Localise with functional imaging first** (somatostatin-receptor imaging such as 68Ga-DOTATATE, or FDG-PET, usually whole-body), then MRI or CT to pinpoint the lesion and plan surgery.
claims.source_text: A systemic approach to tumor localization begins with functional imaging and is followed by anatomic imaging (Table 2, Fig. 2). Functional imaging includes somatostatin receptor imaging (68Ga/64Cu‐DOTATATE, ‐DOTANOC, or ‐DOTATOC, or octreotide scan) and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography []; whole‐body imaging is typically necessary … To confirm tumor localization and plan for surgery, magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography are generally recommended due to their high resolution.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Complete resection is curative and preferred:** plan a wide excision with negative margins. Surgery succeeded in over 90% of patients whose tumour was found.
claims.source_text: TIO is curable if the causative tumor can be completely resected, which is the definitive and preferred treatment … surgery was successful in >90% of these patients … a wide resection with negative tumor margins should be planned.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Pre-operative biopsy is a warning sign:** in one Italian study, every patient biopsied before surgery had a recurrence.
claims.source_text: In a recent Italian study, all patients undergoing lesion biopsy before surgery had tumor recurrence
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Radiofrequency ablation or cryoablation** can be used when a tumour is hard to resect completely; success varies and long-term outcomes are unknown.
claims.source_text: Radiofrequency ablation [, ] or cryoablation [, ] have been used to treat TIO when the location of a tumor has made it difficult to completely resect (Fig. 2), although the success rate is variable [] and long‐term outcomes are unknown.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start medical therapy as soon as the biochemical diagnosis is made,** to limit hungry bone syndrome and prepare the skeleton for surgery.
claims.source_text: Therapy should be initiated as soon as a biochemical diagnosis has been made to minimize HBS and prepare the skeleton for surgery
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Conventional therapy is phosphate salts plus active vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol).** ⚠️ Never give phosphate alone: it drives hyperparathyroidism and works poorly.
claims.source_text: Traditionally, the approach to medical therapy has been conventional therapy: phosphate salts and active vitamin D (calcitriol, alfacalcidol) … It is important not to treat with phosphate salts alone due to their tendency to induce hyperparathyroidism and their limited effectiveness.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Conventional therapy is reasonable while searching for the tumour or awaiting surgery.** For severe symptoms, an unresectable tumour or a non-localisable tumour needing long-term treatment, burosumab may be advantageous.
claims.source_text: Treatment with conventional therapy using active vitamin D and phosphate is a reasonable initial approach during the initial search for a tumor and while awaiting surgical resection, in order to heal the osteomalacia. In the setting of severe hypophosphatemic symptoms, unresectable tumor, or a presumed TIO with a nonlocalizable tumor requiring long‐term treatment, burosumab may be advantageous to provide symptomatic improvement and better biochemical control and healing of osteomalacia, using the protocol described by Jan de Beur et al.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Burosumab (anti-FGF23 antibody) restored phosphate and improved osteomalacia, pain and mobility in phase 2 studies,** but neither it nor conventional therapy halts tumour growth. FGF23 levels cannot be interpreted during burosumab treatment.
claims.source_text: Burosumab, a human monoclonal antibody against FGF23 that blocks the action of FGF23, offers a promising new therapeutic option. It is approved for the treatment of nonresectable/nonlocalizable TIO in the EU, USA, Japan, and China. Two phase 2 studies have demonstrated that burosumab restores phosphate homeostasis and improves osteomalacia, fracture healing, bone pain, functional mobility, and health‐related QoL for patients with TIO [, ]. However, neither burosumab nor phosphate salts with active vitamin D halt tumor progression. … FGF23 levels cannot be interpreted in patients treated with burosumab.
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After resection, watch for hungry bone syndrome** and treat it with calcium and vitamin D. Phosphate usually normalises within 5 days; measure it frequently until normal, then annually.
claims.source_text: The recommended treatment for HBS includes calcium and vitamin D supplementation … Serum phosphate normalization is usually observed within 5 days post‐surgery … Serum phosphate should be measured frequently until normalization and then annually
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Recurrence can come up to 20 years later.** For persistent or recurrent TIO, repeat the full biochemical and imaging work-up to find metastases or multiple foci.
claims.source_text: Tumor recurrence has been reported ≤20 years after initial resection … In persistent and/or recurrent TIO, the diagnostic approach-including the biochemical evaluation, and functional and anatomical imaging-should be repeated to detect metastasis or multiple foci and to exclude other diseases
claims.locator: Jan de Beur SM, Minisola S, Xia W-B et al. (international expert Delphi panel), Journal of Internal Medicine, 'Global guidance for the recognition, diagnosis, and management of tumor-induced osteomalacia', 2023 (vol 293, pp 309–328), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108006/, retrieved 2026-09-23
